newsitem.title: FRANCE: Ponsolle sees banks backing Eurotunnel debt plan.
newsitem.headline: Ponsolle sees banks backing Eurotunnel debt plan.

text.p: Executive chairman Patrick Ponsolle of Channel Tunnel operator Eurotunnel SA/Plc said on Friday he believed creditor banks would back the company's plan to restructure its 70 billion francs ($11.8 billion) of debt.

Shareholders of Anglo-French Eurotunnel massively voted in favour of the debt deal on Thursday, after a stormy meeting in which investors, angered by the company's losses and dive in the share price, heckled and jeered Ponsolle.

Now the 174 lenders have to approve the debt rescue plan, which swaps eight billion francs of debt for Eurotunnel shares and consequently cuts the shareholders' stake to 54.5 percent of the capital from 100.

Ponsolle told Reuters Financial Television that, given the fact that the French and British government had tied a 34-year extension to Eurotunnel's operating licence to 99 years to approval by shareholders and lenders, the banks would back the restructuring plan.
"I think they will approve it," he said.

Ponsolle said he had met a number of the banks in recent weeks and that some were bitter that the plan gave too much to the shareholders, but he said that bitterness matched that of the shareholders who thought the banks were getting a better deal. He thought that indicated the plan was a "good compromise".
But the steering group of banks had not felt any strong opposition from the creditors, he said.
The biggest creditors, Lazards and Merrill Lynch, which both bought Eurotunnel's bank loans on the secondary market, are supportive of the plan, he said.
Lazards has 8.71 percent of the junior bank debt while Merill Lynch has 3.82 percent.
Ponsolle reiterated that Eurotunnel would make a profit in 1997, before interest payments and depreciation, of 50 million pounds ($84.3 million).

Under the terms of the debt deal, banks will get a variety of debt instruments, in addition to shares, to cut Eurotunnel's interest burden by 40 percent over seven years and push out its repayment period to 2050 from 2012.

This will give Eurotunnel breathing space to stabilise its finances while competing in the cross-Channel transport market, in which the ferry companies are waging a savage price war. ($ = 5.926 French Francs) ($ = 0.592 British Pounds)
